parts: Lesson 30: Optional Module B: Role of a Photojournalist — Summary

A good photojournalist is a skilled photographer and a thinking, creative person who mixes technique and judgement to capture images as they happen. Manipulating the image (e.g. making people pose) is wrong: it would no longer be journalism but story telling. Preparedness: be alert and ready to act fast with the camera always at hand, be at the right place at the right time and positioned at the best place with the camera ready. For announced events (sports, political meetings) the photo editor assigns a photojournalist who photographs participants, audience and venue; for events one cannot prepare for (terrorist attack, riot, train accident, earthquake, bridge collapse) the photojournalist must act quickly while ensuring his own safety, and usually captures the aftermath, trying to convey the sense, magnitude and impact of the event.

Only a few pictures are published each day. The photo editor chooses pictures by: the major news events of the day (a photograph enhancing the lead story), the nature of the photograph (hard-hitting, tells a story) and what interests the reader (local events). For a photo feature the photojournalist needs patience and must win the trust of the people photographed, spend time with them and explain the purpose so that they behave naturally.

Ethics are moral principles that govern the practice of journalism. Truthfulness is a core ethic: a photojournalist must always take pictures that tell the truth. In the digital age it is easy to change a photograph (show a man smoking, a crowd that was not there, people in front of foreign monuments). All manipulation of photographs is a violation of basic journalistic ethics; the photojournalist must photograph what happened when it happened and not invent or recreate a situation. Staging a picture by making people pose (children pretending to eat the mid-day meal) is also against ethics.

Photography arrived in India within about two years of its discovery; British photographers took pictures of scenery and monuments; the first war of Independence in 1857 was one of the first incidents of war photography in the world; smaller cameras and political developments around the freedom movement helped photojournalism. Raja Deen Dayal: one of the first notable Indian photojournalists, court photographer during the rule of the sixth Nizam of Hyderabad, left an impressive record of British India. Sunil Janah: political activist and journalist; photographed the transition to independence, partition, tribals, industries, temples and Nehru and Gandhi. Homai Vyarawalla: the first woman photojournalist; first published in 1938 in the Bombay Chronicle; worked for the Illustrated Weekly of India; covered World War II in India; freelancer until 1970. Henri Cartier-Bresson: French; travelled in India in the 1940s; famous photograph of Nehru announcing Gandhiji's death; book Henri Cartier-Bresson in India. Raghu Rai: began in the 1960s in Delhi (Hindustan Times, Statesman), Chief Photographer of India Today; photographs of Indira Gandhi, Mother Teresa, the Bhopal gas tragedy and the Bangladesh war. Prashant Panjiar: self-taught, from Kolkata; chief photographer and associate editor, founding member of Outlook magazine.
